body:
I suggest we modify this to state we need to use a CSPRNG like other requirements.

3.2.4 | [MODIFIED] Verify that opaque session tokens are generated using a secure random function.
-- | --

comments.body:
Current requirements:
| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE | [NIST §](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html) |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **3.2.2** | [MODIFIED] Verify that opaque session tokens possess at least 128 bits of entropy. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 331 | 7.1 |
| **3.2.4** | [MODIFIED] Verify that opaque session tokens are generated using a secure random function. | | ✓ | ✓ | 330 | 7.1 |

Discussed it yesterday with @ryarmst - one option is to merge 3.2.2 and 3.2.4.

@elarlang yes, I think a merge makes sense; the entropy and use of a secure random function are closely linked. 

Consider the combined wording:

> Verify that random tokens representing user sessions are generated using a secure random function and possess at least 128 bits of entropy. 

I use the term "random token" (proposed by @tghosth) to replace "opaque token" due to the varied industry use of the latter (see #2100).

Based on opened issue, Jim would like to see the term CSPRNG in the requirement.
> cryptographically-secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG)

Whoops, I read @jmanico's posted requirement as his recommendation. Updated:

> Verify that random tokens representing user sessions are generated using a CSPRNG and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.

Update:
> Verify that random tokens representing user sessions are generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.

ping @tghosth @jmanico

For OAuth, the spec says:

> The probability of an attacker guessing generated tokens (and other credentials not intended for handling by end users) MUST be less than or equal to 2^(-128) and SHOULD be less than or equal to 2^(-160).

This requirement is consistent with the requirement from OAuth. Would there be any need to suggest 160 bits (or require it for L3)? I think it's probably OK as it is.

Another point which might be worth mentioning is that even if UUIDs are 128 bits long they do not have 128 bits of entropy. UUIDs are very often used for this kind of usage.

@elarlang is it necessary to define CSPRNG inline, or could this go in the appendix?

@randomstuff Do you know the reasoning for the 160 bit recommendation? In terms of UUIDs, I think there are probably many types of generated IDs/tokens where the length along cannot be used to infer entropy.

> Do you know the reasoning for the 160 bit recommendation?

I don't know if there is any reason more than "more is better" :) which is why I guess simply mentioning 128 bits is probably OK here. The 160 recommendation would fit nicely in the [cheatsheets](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html#session-id-entropy).

> In terms of UUIDs, I think there are probably many types of generated IDs/tokens where the length along cannot be used to infer entropy.

Yes but people very often like to use UUIDs as token for some reason (because they are easy to generate, I guess, and because they are used in many tutorials and [guidelines](https://github.com/pilcrowonpaper/copenhagen/issues/26)) and it looks like very much they have 128 bits of entropy.
I prefer to keep it simple and proposal is still valid: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2131#issuecomment-2411465121

For tags:
* 3.2.2 `[MODIFIED, MERGED FROM 3.2.4]`
* 3.2.4 `[DELETED, MERGED TO 3.2.2]`
